ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Geriatric Medicine Consultation — Mary Seacole — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: One-week review with geriatric medicine: home readings confirm stage 2 hypertension; two first-line medicines; comprehensive geriatric assessment of falls, function, mood and social needs

text.paragraph: A 71-year-old woman living alone with blood pressure 184/102 mmHg and morning headaches, without a hypertensive emergency, bilateral knee osteoarthritis, a fall last year and fear of falling. Please see her at her one-week review for a comprehensive geriatric assessment and advice on blood pressure treatment, falls, her knees and her social needs. [S]
Urgency: Soon; at her one-week review. [S]

list.item: Which blood pressure medicines and target do you advise for her, given her age, living alone and fall risk?
What does the falls assessment show, and what should be done about it?
How should we manage her knee osteoarthritis without oral anti-inflammatory medicines?
Are any of her own remedies a problem with the medicines we plan?
What support do you advise for loneliness, mood, the stairs and the cost of care?

text.paragraph: Mrs. Seacole, a 71-year-old woman, is seen at the request of Dr. Fairweather-Kent at her one-week review. A nurse and healer for most of her life, she gives a precise history. Her home readings over seven days average 168/96; her morning headaches are milder. Her knees ache on stairs and rising from a chair. Last year she tripped on the outside steps without injury; since then she goes out less, especially on wet days, and some weeks speaks to few people. She manages her own personal care, medicines and money; heavy shopping is hard. She has paused her liquorice infusion and uses ginger tea and a liniment she makes herself, which she massages into her knees. She is careful with money since a bankruptcy long ago and worries about the cost of medicines and taxis. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: She was born Mary Jane Grant in Kingston, Jamaica, in 1805, the daughter of James Grant, a white Scottish army officer, and a free Black Jamaican woman who kept a boarding house; she was born free, at a time when many Black people in the Caribbean were enslaved, and had a sister, Louisa, and a brother, Edward. In her memoir she wrote that "the century and myself were both young together" and called herself a Creole "with good Scotch blood." [D]
A London commemorative database gives her date of birth as November 23, 1805; English Heritage, the Mary Seacole Trust and her memoir give no day. [D]

Her mother was a healer, "like very many of the Creole women, an admirable doctress," and taught her traditional Jamaican medicine; as a child she practised on her doll, and she later learned "a great deal of Creole medicinal art" in her mother's house. She visited England in the early 1820s and gained some knowledge of European medicine. [D]

She married Edwin Horatio Hamilton Seacole on November 10, 1836, and they kept a store at Black River; he was delicate, she nursed him, and he died in 1844, followed closely by the death of her mother. She had no children. [D]

In 1850 she nursed victims of the cholera epidemic in Kingston, learning about its treatment from a doctor lodging in her house; in 1851 she went to Cruces, on the Isthmus of Panama, where she treated cholera with mustard emetics, warm fomentations, mustard plasters and calomel, and was called the "yellow doctress." [D]

In Cruces she had cholera herself: "I felt an unpleasant chill come over me … and, before nightfall, I knew full well that my turn had come at last, and that the cholera had attacked me." She recovered. [D]

In 1853 she cared for victims of a yellow fever epidemic in Kingston; she was invited by the medical authorities to supervise nursing at Up-Park Camp, the British Army's headquarters, and turned her mother's former lodging house into a hospital. [D]

At the outbreak of the Crimean War she went to London and asked the War Office to send her as an army nurse; she was refused. She paid her own way to the Crimea and, with Thomas Day, a relative of her husband, built the British Hotel at Spring Hill near Balaclava, a place of respite for sick and recovering soldiers; she nursed the wounded on the battlefield, sometimes under fire, and soldiers called her "Mother Seacole." [D]

She returned from the Crimea in 1856 in poor health and poor finances; in her memoir she wrote: "I returned from it shaken in health … a little labour fatigues me now--I cannot watch by sick-beds as I could--a week's want of rest quite knocks me up now." She described herself as "a hearty, strong woman--plain-spoken people might say stout." [D]

With unpaid bills and unsold stock at the end of the war, she was declared bankrupt in November 1856. The Times and Punch campaigned for her, a Seacole Fund Grand Military Festival was held in Kennington in July 1857, and her autobiography, Wonderful Adventures of Mrs. Seacole in Many Lands, was published the same month. [D]

W. H. Russell, war correspondent of The Times, wrote of her in 1857: "I trust that England will not forget one who nursed her sick, who sought out her wounded to aid and succour them, and who performed the last offices for some of her illustrious dead." [D]

She travelled between England and Jamaica in the 1860s and was back in London by about 1869 to 1870, where she mixed with royalty and acted as a personal masseuse to the Princess of Wales; she was painted by Albert Charles Challen around 1869 and sculpted by Count Gleichen in 1871. [D]
Her last known photograph was taken around 1873; little else is documented about her health or daily life in her last decade in London. [D]

Her memoir describes her lifelong practice of nursing and healing, including the remedies she carried, and her belief that the Creoles seek out "the simple remedies which are available for the terrible diseases": "beside the nettle ever grows the cure for its sting." [D]

list.item: Blood pressure medicines and target (I10). Stage 2 hypertension, confirmed at home, with ECG evidence of left ventricular hypertrophy and a 10-year cardiovascular risk of about 14%. She is fit, independent and has no orthostatic drop, so the target of below 130/80 mmHg applies to her as to younger adults, reached gradually. Start two first-line medicines: amlodipine 5 mg and chlorthalidone 12.5 mg. In a 71-year-old woman a thiazide can lower sodium, especially when she eats little, so check sodium and potassium in about four weeks, check standing pressure at every visit, and teach a sick-day rule to stop chlorthalidone if she cannot eat or drink normally. If sodium falls, stop it and use an angiotensin receptor blocker instead. An echocardiogram is reasonable for stage 2 hypertension with ECG voltage. [S]

Falls (Z91.81). STEADI shows high risk: a fall last year, fear of falling, a Timed Up and Go of 15 seconds, a below-average chair stand and poor tandem balance. No orthostatic drop, no sedating or anticholinergic medicines, and her vision is adequate. The stairs to her rooms and worn slip-on shoes are the main hazards. Strength and balance exercise reduces falls in community-dwelling older adults. [S]

Knee osteoarthritis (M17.0). Clinical bilateral knee osteoarthritis; imaging is not needed. Exercise therapy, then tai chi, topical diclofenac, weight loss of at least 5%, and a cane in the right hand are all strongly recommended. Avoid oral anti-inflammatory medicines, which raise blood pressure and harm the kidneys. An intra-articular corticosteroid injection is an option for a flare. Her own massage is welcome and fits the exercise plan. [S]

Her own remedies. Liquorice root contains glycyrrhizin, which raises blood pressure and lowers potassium; that would add to the potassium loss from chlorthalidone, so pausing it is wise. Ginger tea in food amounts is fine. Her liniment contains camphor and methyl salicylate; used on one knee, or at a different time from the diclofenac gel, and never under a heat pad, it is safe. Her knowledge of her remedies is good, and she should be asked about any new one rather than told to stop. [S]

Mood, loneliness, home and costs. PHQ-9 of 6 reflects loneliness and fear of falling rather than depression. A social prescribing link worker, a tai chi group and a lunch club address loneliness and falls together. An occupational therapy home visit for a stair rail and bath board. Generic medicines in 90-day supplies, a free blood pressure monitor and help with transport keep costs down. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Fairweather-Kent's note. Clinic readings 184/102 last week and 176/98 today; home seven-day average 168/96. ECG with left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage. Sodium 140, potassium 4.1, creatinine 0.92 mg/dL (eGFR 67), glucose 96, hemoglobin A1c 5.6%, total cholesterol 228, LDL 146, HDL 54, triglycerides 140 mg/dL, TSH 2.1, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 18 mg/g, hemoglobin 12.8. Knee pain 6 out of 10; KOOS JR 52.5. PHQ-9 6 today. [S]

list.item: Amlodipine 5 mg and chlorthalidone 12.5 mg each morning; target below 130/80 mmHg. [S]
Sodium, potassium and creatinine in about four weeks; standing blood pressure at every visit; sick-day rule for chlorthalidone; if sodium falls, stop it and use an angiotensin receptor blocker. [S]
Echocardiogram. [S]
Physical therapy for strength, balance and the knees, then tai chi; a cane in the right hand; firm closed shoes. [S]
Occupational therapy home visit for the stairs and bathroom. [S]
Diclofenac gel; no oral anti-inflammatory medicines; a corticosteroid injection as an option for a flare; aim for 5% weight loss. [S]
Keep liquorice paused while on treatment; ginger tea and her liniment are fine as she uses them. [S]
Social prescribing link worker, tai chi group and lunch club; check of help with costs and transport. [S]
Statin decision with her at the four-week review. [S]
Discussed with Dr. Fairweather-Kent, who saw her the same day. The plan was explained to Mrs. Seacole, who asked detailed questions about the medicines as a nurse would and agreed to each part. [S]
Follow-up: Dr. Fairweather-Kent continues her care. Geriatric medicine is available if she falls, her sodium falls or her blood pressure is hard to control. [S]
